extracted.intended_audience: learned readers/students of medieval natural philosophy, natural historians, and practitioners of the liberal arts (Latin-reading scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition from a medieval/renaissance natural-philosophy/encyclopedic treatise collecting criteria, causes, and recommended study order for sciences, medicines, technical arts, and public spectacles. The text gives both explanatory theory and prescriptive guidance (e.g., how to learn, how to diagnose, how to perform tightrope acts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended sequence of study to attain wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclidem primó; inde Alchindum ad firmandà imaginationem aggrediemur; postea Calculatoré; Arithmetica; Archimedem, Apollonium & Eutocium; inde Scotum cum Aristotele & interpretibus (Theophrasto, Alexandro, Themistio, Simplicio, Philopono, Averroes); sextò Prolemeum, septimù Vitruuium; inde ad quam voluerimus artem profiteri (medicam, iurisprudentiam, theologiam) tranfibimus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recommended curriculum: begin with Euclid to form geometrical understanding, then proceed through arithmetic and the major mathematicians and commentators, then the liberal arts and finally professional specializations. The list is prescriptive: follow this order to acquire 'sapientia' and to make imagination and calculation steady.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of extensive demonstrative writing in mathematics and poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicis; quia solum probatur quod sine his habent; & qui ad demonstrationem necessaria sunt — etsi ob id etsi multo plura sciret Euclides & Archimedes quam scripserint; laudatur magis qui plura scripserit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises authors who provide many demonstrative or extensive works (Euclid, Archimedes) — in both mathematics and poetry more voluminous, demonstrative output is prized. For evaluation: quantity plus demonstrative clarity raise esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style criterion for oratory: natural subtlety versus affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtilitas in oratione; affectata molestia est, quae sponte fluit in oratione, jucundissima. In hismanquam naturam dum imitatur, ab septimo artis suspicione discedit, & liquidior fluit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oratorical subtlety that flows naturally is pleasant; affected, artificial mannerisms are displeasing. The advice: imitate nature, avoid forced affectation; aim for fluidity and clarity in speech. (The passage contrasts types of subtlety and warns against overly contrived divisions and artifices.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical diagnostic criteria from urine
rubrics_metrics.description: Urina continet sedimentum sola; in ima tantum parte hoc prope adumbrat eam; pars quae sedimentum continet a pura illubibét; urina tenuis valde subtilitatis ob calorem; urina ventris inflationi prodest; quando urina turbata, pinguedo, congestio, temperaturae, & sedimento indicant morbid states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use urine qualities (sediment location, clarity, thinness, heat, turbidity, fatness) to diagnose humoral states and illnesses. The text gives causal reasoning (heat/thinness => penetration; turbidity => presence of earthy/pinguedinous matter) and implications for prognosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three principal faculties of living beings (analytical rubric for biological description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Viua ipse praeter hunc latentem sensum habent facultates principales tres: generationem; nutritionem; augmentum. Quatuor his servientes: attractionem, retentricem, concoquientem (concoquit), et expultrix (expultrix vel retentrix, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing living bodies, classify operations into primary faculties (generation, nourishment, growth) and secondary operations (attraction/assimilation, retention, concoction/digestion, expulsion). Use these categories to analyze physiology and causes of functions/diseases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of motor learning and habit formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Motus duobus constant principiis: altero quod omne animal etiam imperfectum habet virtute (instinct, drives); reliquum est genus memoriae sive habitus. Infantes et rudes discunt per consuetudinem; corpus contrahe musculos proprios per repetitio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning motor actions requires (1) natural appetitive/instinctive power and (2) acquired habit/memory. Practical implication: repetition and gradual practice are necessary for developing coordinated motion; observation of infants supports this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes and criteria for fatigue when ascending (ascent vs. plane)
rubrics_metrics.description: Causa laboris in ascendendo triplex est: (1) communis omni motui quia musculi et membra moventur; (2) quia ascendendo per scalas cogitur elevatio maior per gradum ergo corpus fit gravius; (3) in acclivi superficie pedes non quiescunt recte ergo cogitur alteratio positionis et magnus labor musculorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate difficulty of a climb, consider muscular movement, per-step elevation, and foot stability on the incline. Experimentally, higher steps or steeper inclines increase fatigue; design of stairs/ramps should account for these three causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for successful tightrope performance (funambulism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Funambulus opus est: certa proportione ponderum (sensim pondus compensans), baculus (pole) ad sensum & pondera distribuenda, manus & brachia idoneae vires, exercitatione et habitu; keep body intentus (focused), avoid sudden extension or retraction, maintain center and not panic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed performing rules: establish the correct ratio of counterweights and pole length; practice extension/retraction of arms slowly; cultivate steadiness (non-pavar), ensure foot placement and soles adapted, use poles or appended weights as needed. The text lists many device-variations (boards, planks, appended disks) and emphasizes training and proportion over mere daring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical preconditions for performing spectacular mechanical feats (mirabilia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mirabilia are often produced by mechanical arrangement (hidden chambers, counterweights, calculated levers), by exploiting material properties (metals, sulphur, bitumen), and by practiced manual dexterity; their reception depends on novelty, cost, social status of performer, and claims of divine assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating public spectacles: document the concealed mechanisms (e.g., hidden grooves or chambers, sequences of weights), anticipate public suspicion (laws, accusations of sorcery), and recognize that social context affects perceived value. Practical advice: many feats are reproducible with technique and instruments rather than miracle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical mechanical principle: impact and fracture depending on support and speed
rubrics_metrics.description: If a stone or hammer strikes an object supported on a plane with another support, the struck piece will fracture more easily when the striking motion is faster and the relative sizes/positions of supports favor impulse transfer; motus tempore indiget (motion needs duration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For experimental demonstrations of strength and fracture: control support geometry, striking speed, and lever arms. Faster strikes and larger effective moment cause easier breakage; this explains how small strikes at high speed can shatter supported stone or clay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical/structural considerations for rope rupture under repeated wrapping
rubrics_metrics.description: A rope can be severed by repeated wrapping/rotation around a fixed nail with the hand drawing it such that the vibrating impulse and the last circumnavigation focus stress where the rope abuts the nail; when the intermediate material is softer and the hand is strong and the impulse quick, the rope splits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers and performers should note that local abrasion, concentrated curvature and rapid impulse produce rope failure; to avoid accidents, ensure appropriate rope thickness, minimize abrasive contact points, and avoid rapid repeated friction against a sharp anchorage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy and antipathy as criteria for predicting animal/human reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sympathiam voco consensum rerum absque manifesta ratione: velut antipathiam, ut lacerta homini gaudeat; non est explicita ratio, but prior sight or impression may cause animals or people to react as if they had seen a wolf etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forecasting behavior, include non-obvious sympathetic/antipathetic relations: prior impressions, odors, or partial resemblance can provoke fear or attraction. This is a heuristic used in natural-history observations, not strict causal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of 'miracle' versus craft — social and legal determinants
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracles lose esteem because (1) they are associated with cheap/trivial arts; (2) performed by lowly persons; (3) ascribed to divine aid and therefore suspect or condemned by law; (4) princes disappointed by previous deceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To appraise a spectacle's social value: consider performer status, perceived source (natural art vs divine), cost and accessibility. The text argues this explains why true ars often receives little honor despite ingenuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical construction principle: deriving spherical proportions from planar constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Typographica arti — from plane to solid: propose how greater circles and divisions yield spherical proportions; e.g., ‘‘In sphaera habet sinus… eius est quarta pars diametri…’’ and procedures to obtain the sphere from planar diagrams by division into circles and arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological advice for geometers and typographers: construct spheres by planar decomposition into circles with known ratios; use Euclidean measurement and subdivisions to infer spherical arcs. This serves as a technical rubric for drafting spherical figures with small error.
